preamble: Insertion of a palatal nasal [ɲ] in a hiatus whose first vowel is a nasalized [ĩ]. In medieval Galician-Portuguese, the loss of intervocalic /n/ left nasal vowels in hiatus (Latin vīnum > vĩo), and after [i] the nasality was re-articulated as a consonant: a palatal nasal was inserted between the two vowels, giving vinho, minha, galinha. Basque shows a parallel development: where intervocalic *n had been lost leaving a nasal vowel, a nasal stop was restored, and after /i/ the restored consonant is a palatal ñ rather than the etymological apico-alveolar n (common Basque katea vs. Souletin kathiña 'chain').

examples.note: Intervocalic /n/ was lost after nasalizing the preceding vowel; the nasal [ĩ] then developed a palatal nasal consonant inserted between the two vowels. Medieval spellings vỹo and vinno coexist in the texts.
Here the nasality came from the initial m-, yet the same palatal nasal was inserted after nasal [ĩ].
Galician shares the insertion of ñ after nasal [ĩ] with Portuguese (also galiña 'hen', miña 'my').

examples.from: Latin catēna, with loss of intervocalic n (common Basque katea)
examples.note: After loss of intervocalic *n the nasality survived on the vowels; where a nasal stop was later restored after /i/, it surfaced as palatal ñ instead of the etymological n.
